t: Why Kindness Is A Powerful Classroom Management Strategy agement-strategy/
q: You see, students are accustomed to having anger and frustration attached to accountability. They’re used to teachers enforcing consequences with an air of revenge or reciprocity.
Which encourages them to deny responsibility for their misbehavior. It encourages them to argue and point the finger elsewhere.
If, however, they receive a consequence from someone they like and respect, and it’s given impersonally , then the response is quite different.
They’ll accept and even agree with your consequence. They’ll take responsibility, naturally and without you having to say another word.
Your steady, day-after-day consistency , in both personality and commitment to accountability, has a transformational effect on students.
It proves to them that when you enforce a consequence, it’s done purely, and from a caring heart. It proves to them that you’re a leader worth following.
x: He argues that students are accustomed to teachers enforcing consequences with an undertone of anger or revenge, which prompts them to deny responsibility and argue defensively as a form of counter-revenge.

He argues that students are accustomed to teachers enforcing consequences with an undertone of anger or revenge, which prompts them to deny responsibility and argue defensively as a form of counter-revenge.
When a well-liked teacher instead delivers consequences impersonally and without relish, students respond very differently.
A well-liked teacher who delivers consequences impersonally causes students to accept responsibility naturally.
Over time, this combination of kindness and consistency transforms even difficult students into cooperative, respectful ones.

Building on a prior article about consistent accountability paired with kindheartedness, Linsin explains why students so predictably transform into friendlier, more polite versions of themselves once this combination is in place.

q: Every day at school, we are inundated with dozens of emails, hundreds of conversations, and any professional reading we decide to do on top of that. If you're a person who enjoys informational reading or viewing in the evenings (or just surfing the Internet or social media), this info-intake continues well into the night, ending in some cases just prior to going to bed.

There is a vast gap between being knowledgeable and teaching well. The former may enhance the latter, but the latter wholly animates the former; it transforms the dry bones of knowledge into a living, breathing thing. Teaching well, I think, lies in the ability to leverage our knowledge and experience toward making good instructional and relational decisions — and that's wisdom.

Take time to just get away and write — and no, you don't need to write about the latest line you just heard from The Gurus. Write about whatever you want: about what this conference has taught you about yourself, about teaching, about people, about information overload, etc.

People ought to use good subject lines when they email you, and a good subject line gives you a reasonable idea of what's going to be in the email. This allows you to decide if you will open or delete the email.

Sometimes it's not possible, as a participant in a meeting, to keep things moving along (think: whole staff meeting), but in the case of smaller meetings, there is often wasted time that is within your control to minimize. For example, did you really need to share that anecdote from your classroom last week?

The key here is limiting your time because this stuff is like email but with a lower percentage of usefulness. I know there are those of you out there who use Twitter or SnapFace for professional development domination, but for the rest of us, these things flood our minds with tiny bits of information and, in my estimation, cripple our ability to think.
x: Written as he headed to the NCTE conference, Stuart argues that teachers are drowning in information from email, meetings, professional reading and social media, and that more information does not make a better teacher.
Eliot's distinction between information, knowledge and wisdom, arguing that teaching well lies in turning knowledge and experience into good instructional and relational decisions.
His one 'Conference Truth' is that skipping sessions is not a failure, and he reframes a conference around meeting good ideas, other teachers and time alone to write.
For email he recommends deleting on the strength of the subject line, pruning subscriptions and checking only at lunch and before going home, while admitting he struggles to follow his own advice.
He puts part of the responsibility for wasted meeting time on participants, asking whether a classroom anecdote actually advances the meeting.
Social media is presented as email with a lower share of usefulness, which floods teachers with fragments and weakens their capacity to think.

q: In our era of complex teacher evaluation systems, book-length observation rubrics, and “data warehouses,” you and I are almost commanded to define ourselves by external measures. While I certainly accept the ease with which I can deceive myself (and therefore the need for external feedback on how I'm teaching or living), I am equally aware of the ease with which I can fool most people into thinking I'm better at things than I actually am.

This, by the way, is what the system is presently destined to create: inauthentic performances where teachers teach how they think they are supposed to teach so that they can get a teacher evaluation score that means they get to keep their job.
The teacher driven simply to get a Highly Effective evaluation score is unlikely to flourish as much long-term as the teacher driven simply to be as excellent as he can be at his calling.

Why do I think these things are true? We're finite creatures with finite mental energies. Effort expended on attaining a five out of five on element 3.E.w of the Ninety-Two Dimensions of Great Teaching rubric is effort that cannot be expended thinking or reading deeply about what assessment is good for.
You can obsess about being a great teacher, or about looking like one — you can't obsess about both.

The thing is, external validation isn't ultimate; it makes a wretched Top Priority and a horrible god. Again and again, it seems like the people who live the best lives and do the most important work are those for whom external validation is a side effect of an internal quest for excellence.
Spend less time reading your teacher eval rubric and more time reading good books, talking to smart people, and thinking about great teaching.
x: Stuart argues that current evaluation systems almost command teachers to define themselves by external measures, producing inauthentic performances on observation days.
Stuart argues that current evaluation systems almost command teachers to define themselves by external measures, producing inauthentic performances on observation days.
Externalism undermines growth everywhere: grade-chasing students and rating-chasing teachers flourish less than those pursuing real excellence.
Because mental energy is finite, a teacher can obsess about being great or about looking great, but not both.
His practical advice is to spend less time on evaluation rubrics and more on good books, smart people and thinking about great teaching.
External validation is good, he concludes, but it makes a wretched top priority, and the best lives treat it as a side effect of an internal quest for excellence, as John Wooden did.

t: How To Have A Nicer, Friendlier Class
q: Teachers tend to respond in one of two ways. Either they get angry and demand civility through lectures, threats, talking-tos, and how-dare-yous. Or they overwhelm their students with kindness.
The first will cause your students to dislike you. It will cause behind-the-back rebelliousness and resentment. It will bring tension into your classroom and cause more incivility, not less.
The problem with the second approach is that your students won’t respect you. They’ll view you as a pushover. You’ll be brushed aside, if not run over.
To improve the civility in your classroom, you must combine a kind, easygoing disposition with a faithful and unwavering commitment to accountability.
This sends the message that while rudeness and disrespect toward you or their fellow classmates won’t be tolerated, even a sliver, it isn’t personal.
x: Demanding civility through lectures and threats alone tends to increase resentment and behind-the-back rebellion.
Both approaches fail, he argues — the first breeds resentment and rebellion, while the second causes students to lose respect and view the teacher as a pushover.
Both approaches fail, he argues — the first breeds resentment and rebellion, while the second causes students to lose respect and view the teacher as a pushover.
His proposed solution is to combine both qualities simultaneously: a kind, easygoing disposition paired with faithful, unwavering accountability.
This combination communicates that disrespect won't be tolerated, but that consequences are never personal, and that forgiveness is always extended the next day.

t: When Your State Reduces Your Profession to a Test Score
q: Before I move on, let me suggest that what's worth focusing on here isn't the particular state or scoring system, but rather the effects of the system on this particular educator. I would argue that this particular teacher's situation is being experienced in various shades and systems across the United States. That's why I think it's worth today's article.

Here it is: if I am teaching my heart out, growing each year, and earnestly working toward the long-term flourishing of my students, then I will refuse to allow any person in power to cause me to lose sleep at night with a flawed or — what in your case sounds like — insane policy.

In short, a system that would fire me for being a great teacher who happened to have students opt out or make bubble patterns on Testing Days is a system that will inevitably destroy itself. That breaks my heart primarily for the kids and communities involved. And it infuriates my heart because hard-working, earnest, problem-solving teachers like you and me will inevitably leave such systems, which is needless.

But here's how I see it: if I’m an average person, I get to live 70-some years. That is not a long time. It is a time too precious for allowing some external entity to take a single one and drain it of joy. I may not have the power to affect policy, but I do have power to protect my internal life from that policy's pernicious effects. If Viktor Frankl could find meaning in his circumstances, surely there is a way for you and me.
If you lose your job in this way or are judged poorly in this manner, it says nothing about you and everything about the system that fires you and the hearts who judge you.

And D, take heart, because this will not last forever. There is a restoring force with every pendulum, and so too with education policy. What we'll care about in twenty years is whether we worked hard and cultivated joy in the midst of these times.

All I can see to do is keep teaching, keep wrestling with connecting the dots between my kids today and their flourishing in twenty years, keep working toward improving my craft, keep a long-term lens on the work, and keep encouraging one another. And keep reminding you, dear reader, that no matter the times we live in, teaching is still and always will be a noble calling.
x: Responding to a New York teacher whose evaluation hinges on a state growth score she cannot control, Stuart offers a counsel of internal resilience rather than a policy fix.
He argues that a teacher who is teaching wholeheartedly, growing each year and working toward students' long-term flourishing should refuse to let a flawed policy cost them sleep.
He predicts that systems which fire great teachers over opt-outs and bubble patterns will drive good teachers away and ultimately destroy themselves.
Drawing on Viktor Frankl, he separates the power to change policy from the power to protect one's internal life from its pernicious effects.
A poor rating from an algorithmic system, he says, reveals more about the system and its judges than about the teacher.
He argues that a teacher who is teaching wholeheartedly, growing each year and working toward students' long-term flourishing should refuse to let a flawed policy cost them sleep.
Policy pendulums have a restoring force, so what will matter in twenty years is whether teachers worked hard and cultivated joy in hard times.

t: Is It Ever Okay For Students To Leave Their Seat Without Permission? eat-without-permission/
q: The solution is to define for your students precisely and narrowly what is and isn’t okay and when it is and isn’t okay to do it.
You would then model what getting a tissue looks like—which would include taking a direct route to and from the tissue box without interrupting others.
Explicit modeling lays it all out, puts it on record, and removes any excuse to be up and out of their seats for any other reason or in any other way.
Finally, it’s important that you detail any time or times you don’t want them to be able to get up, like while you’re giving directions or providing instruction, for example.
Narrow definitions and precise modeling are the keys to successfully allowing reasonable exceptions to your rules.
As long as you hold accountable any student who strays even a nanometer from your narrow exceptions, you’ll have a more focused and peaceful classroom.
x: His solution is precision: define narrowly and explicitly which actions are exceptions to the raise-your-hand rule, and model exactly what performing them correctly.
Responding to a frequently asked question, Linsin explains how to handle the tension between rigid raise-your-hand rules and reasonable exceptions like getting a tissue or sharpening a pencil.
Explicit modeling of both correct and incorrect ways to perform an exception removes ambiguity and excuses.
Teachers should also specify times when even approved exceptions are off-limits, such as during direct instruction.
His solution is precision: define narrowly and explicitly which actions are exceptions to the raise-your-hand rule, and model exactly what performing them correctly.

He recommends limiting exceptions to just three or four commonly requested needs, spending about thirty minutes teaching and modeling them, and then holding students strictly accountable for any deviation.

t: Character Strengths, Integrity, and My Three-Year-Old
q: As Laura's father, my desire is that gratitude be well-developed in her, both externally (in the habit of saying “thank you”) and internally (in the habit of focusing on all she has versus all she doesn't). I want these things for Laura not because I look like a good dad when she says “Thank you,” but because external gratitude will make her a blessing to others and internal gratitude is a great source of motivation. In short, I want Laura to live a flourishing life, and gratitude is one of the surest means toward that.

If you're going to teach character strengths well, you've got to have experiential knowledge about what you're talking about. This lends to your teacher credibility, which John Hattie's “Visible Learning” meta-analysis has found to be a significant factor in student outcomes (effect size .90, as found in Visible Learning for Teachers).
Just as growth mindset is a journey, so, too, is the consistent life, the life devoid of hypocrisy, the life where the character strengths we teach are the ones we master daily.

When I say I want to live an integrated life — a life of integrity — it certainly means that I hope to be honest and morally upright, but even more than that it means that I want to iron out the seams in my life. I want there to be less of a jarring sensation when I see a student in the local grocery store while I'm with my wife and children, or when my friends from church see me interact with my relatives or my colleagues. In short, I want to be like an integer in math class, a “whole number”; I want to be consistent.

Or let me bring it to a place that every teacher can relate to: I want the conversations I have about students and colleagues and bosses to be the kinds of conversations I wouldn't be humiliated to have broadcasted for the world to see. I know my own tendency to speak in private like I never would in public — and that bothers me not just from the obvious moral standpoint, but also from the performance standpoint. And my goal with this paragraph is to produce introspection, not guilt.

What mental energies do I unconsciously spend keeping my stories straight and my multiple selves correctly hidden or displayed? How much more force might we bring to bear on problems in our classrooms or our homes if we weren't undermining the people we're working to become, the legacies we're hoping to leave, with small, self-deceiving excuses (“Well, I'll just neglect this one thank you note a bit longer,” or, “I'm just joking around with my friends — it's harmless.”)

This is because they spend huge swaths of their academic lives engaged in a dizzying array of tasks that target a mind-numbing myriad of standards. I think this creates a school day that is mildly entertaining, depending on the teacher, but ultimately senseless. This experience, I would argue, is so dis-integrated that it functionally aids in the disintegration of our students' minds.
x: Stuart opens with rehearsing gratitude with his three-year-old and realizing he owed a thank-you note he had neglected for months, then turns the moment into an argument about teaching character strengths.
Stuart argues that teachers should only teach the character strengths they are actively working on themselves, because experience drives credibility.
Stuart argues that teachers should only teach the character strengths they are actively working on themselves, because experience drives credibility.
He reclaims integrity in its root sense of wholeness, aiming for a life with fewer seams between how one acts with students, family, church and colleagues.
Talking about students and colleagues in private as one never would in public costs not only morally but in performance, by draining mental energy.
Such integration, he argues, frees mental energy that self-deception and multiple selves consume.
